Seeing thy\narmy fly away from Bhimasena, the mighty Karna, O king, rallied it with\ngreat efforts. The mighty-armed Karna, having rallied thy son's host,\nproceeded against the Pandavas, those heroes difficult of defeat in\nbattle. The great car-warriors of the Pandavas also, shaking their bows\nand shooting their shafts, proceeded against the son of Radha. Bhimasena,\nand the grandson of Sini, and Shikhandi and Janamejaya, and\nDhrishtadyumna of great strength, and all the Prabhadrakas, and those\ntigers among men, the Pancalas, filled with rage and inspired with desire\nof victory, rushed in that battle from every side against thy army.\nSimilarly, the great car-warriors of thy army, O king, quickly proceeded\nagainst the Pandava host, desirous of slaughtering it. Teeming with cars\nand elephants and horses, and abounding with foot-soldiers and standards,\nthe two armies then, O tiger among men, assumed a wonderful aspect.\nShikhandi proceeded against Karna, and Dhrishtadyumna proceeded against\nthy son Duhshasana, accompanied by a large force. Nakula proceeded\nagainst Vrishasena, while Yudhishthira against Citrasena. Sahadeva, O\nking, in that battle, proceeded against Uluka. Satyaki proceeded against\nShakuni, and the sons of Draupadi against the other Kauravas. The mighty\ncar-warrior Ashvatthama proceeded, with great care, against Arjuna.\nSharadvata's son Kripa proceeded against the mighty bowman Yudhamanyu,\nwhile Kritavarma of great strength proceeded against Uttamauja. The\nmighty-armed Bhimasena, O sire, alone and unsupported, resisted all the\nKurus and thy sons at the head of their division. The slayer of Bhishma,\nShikhandi, then, O monarch, with his winged arrows, resisted Karna,\ncareering fearlessly in that battle. Held in check, Karna then, his lips\ntrembling in rage, assailed Shikhandi with three arrows in the midst of\nhis eyebrows. With those three arrows sticking on his forehead, Shikhandi\nlooked highly beautiful like a silver mountain with three elevated\ncrests. Deeply pierced by the Suta's son in that encounter, the mighty\nbowman Shikhandi pierced Karna, in return, with ninety keen shafts. The\nmighty car-warrior Karna then, slaying Shikhandi's steeds and next his\ndriver with three arrows, cut off his standard with a razor-faced arrow.\nThat mighty car-warrior then, that scorcher of foes, filled with rage,\njumped down from his steedless car and hurled a dart at Karna. Cutting\noff that dart with three shafts in that encounter, Karna then, O Bharata,\npierced Shikhandi with nine keen arrows. Avoiding then the shafts sped\nfrom Karna's bow, that best of men, Shikhandi, exceedingly mangled,\nretreated speedily from that spot. Then Karna, O monarch, began to\nscatter the troops of the Pandavas, like a mighty wind scattering a heap\nof cotton. Meanwhile Dhrishtadyumna, O monarch, afflicted by thy son,\npierced Duhshasana, in return, with three arrows in the centre of the\nchest. Then Duhshasana, O sire, pierced his assailant's left arm with a\nbroad-headed shaft, sharp and straight and equipped with wings of gold.\nThus pierced, Dhrishtadyumna, filled with wrath and the desire to\nretaliate, sped a terrible shaft, O Bharata, at Duhshasana. Thy son,\nhowever, O king, with three shafts of his, cut off that impetuous arrow\nsped by Dhrishtadyumna as it coursed towards him. Approaching\nDhrishtadyumna then, he struck him in the arms and the chest with\nseventeen other broad-headed shafts adorned with gold. Thereat Prishata's\nson, filled with rage, cut off Duhshasana's bow, O sire, with a sharp\nrazor-headed arrow, at which all the troops there uttered a loud shout.\nTaking up then another bow, thy son, as if smiling, held Dhrishtadyumna\nin check with showers of arrows from every side. Beholding the prowess of\nthat high-souled son of thine, the combatants, as also the Siddhas and\nthe Apsaras, became all filled with wonder. We then saw the mighty\nDhrishtadyumna thus assailed by Duhshasana to resemble a huge elephant,\nheld in check by a lion. Then many Pancala car-warriors and elephants and\nhorses, O elder brother of Pandu, desirous of rescuing the commander (of\nthe Pandava army) encompassed thy son. The battle that commenced, O\nscorcher of foes, between thy warriors and the enemy, presented as\nfrightful a sight as that which may be seen at the destruction of all\ncreatures at the end of the Yuga.\n\n\"'Vrishasena, staying by the side of his father, having pierced Nakula\nwith five arrows made wholly of iron, pierced him once again with three\nother arrows. The heroic Nakula then, as if smiling, deeply pierced\nVrishasena in the chest with a cloth-yard shaft of great keenness. Thus\npierced by his mighty foe, that scorcher of foes, viz., Vrishasena,\npierced his assailant with twenty arrows and was himself pierced by him\nwith five. Then those two bulls among men shrouded each other with\nthousands of arrows, at which the divisions that supported them broke.\nBeholding the troops of Dhritarashtra's son flying away, the Suta's son,\nfollowing them, O king, began to forcibly stop them. After Karna had gone\naway, Nakula proceeded against the Kauravas. Karna's son also, avoiding\nNakula, proceeded quickly, O sire, to where his father, the son of Radha,\nwas for protecting his car-wheel."

Uluka then, that delighter of his father, jumping down\nfrom his car, O king, quickly proceeded and entered the division of the\nTrigartas. Satyaki, having pierced Shakuni with twenty keen arrows,\neasily cut off the standard of Subala's son with a broad-headed arrow.\nThe valiant son of Subala, filled with rage, O king, in that encounter,\npierced Satyaki's armour and then cut off his golden standard. Then\nSatyaki pierced him in return with many keen arrows, and struck his\ndriver, O monarch, with three arrows. With great speed then, he\ndespatched with other shafts the steeds of Shakuni to Yama's abode.\nSpeedily alighting then, O bull among men, from his car, Shakuni, that\nmighty car-warrior, quickly ascended the car of Uluka. The latter then\nbore away with great speed his father from Sini's grandson, that warrior\nskilled in battle. Then Satyaki, O king, rushed in that battle against\nthy army with great impetuosity, at which that army broke. Shrouded with\nthe arrows of Sini's grandson, thy army, O monarch, fled away on all\nsides with great speed, and fell down deprived of life.\n\n\"'Thy son resisted Bhimasena in that battle, in a trice Bhima made that\nruler of men steedless and driverless and carless and standardless, at\nwhich the (Pandava) troops became highly glad. Then thy son, O king, went\naway from Bhimasena's presence. The whole Kuru army, at this, rushed\nagainst Bhimasena. Tremendous became the din made by those combatants\ninspired with the desire of slaying Bhimasena. Yudhamanyu, piercing\nKripa, quickly cut off his bow. Then Kripa, that foremost of all wielders\nof weapons, taking up another bow, felled Yudhamanyu's standard and\ndriver and umbrella on the Earth. At this, the mighty car-warrior\nYudhamanyu retreated on his car, driving it himself. Uttamauja covered\nthe terrible son of Hridika, endued with terrible prowess, with a thick\nshower of arrows like a cloud pouring torrents of rain on a mountain. The\nbattle between them, O scorcher of foes, became so awful that its like, O\nmonarch, I had never seen before. Then Kritavarma, O king, in that\nencounter, suddenly pierced Uttamauja in the chest, at which the latter\nsat down on the terrace of his car. His driver then bore away that\nforemost of car-warriors. Then the whole Kuru army rushed at Bhimasena.\nDuhshasana and Subala's son, encompassing the son of Pandu with a large\nelephant force, began to strike him with small arrows. Then Bhima,\ncausing the wrathful Duryodhana to turn his back on the field by means of\nhundreds of arrows, quickly rushed towards that elephant force. Beholding\nthat elephant-force advance impetuously against him, Vrikodara became\nfilled with great rage and invoked his celestial weapons. And he began to\nstrike elephants with elephants like Indra striking the Asuras. While\nengaged in slaughtering those elephants, Vrikodara, in that battle,\ncovered the welkin with his shafts like myriads of insects covering a\nfire. Like the wind scattering masses of clouds, Bhima quickly scattered\nand destroyed crowds of elephants united together in thousands. Covered\nall over with networks of gold, as also with many gems, the elephants\nlooked exceedingly beautiful in that battle like clouds charged with\nlightning. Slaughtered by Bhima, those elephants, O king, began to fly\naway. Some amongst them, with their hearts pierced, fell down on the\nEarth. With those fallen and failing elephants adorned with gold, the\nEarth looked beautiful there, as if strewn with broken mountains. With\nthe fallen elephant-warriors of blazing resplendence and adorned with\ngems, the Earth looked beautiful as if strewn with planets of exhausted\nmerit. Then elephants, with their temples, frontal globes, and trunks\ndeeply pierced, fled in hundreds in that battle, afflicted with the\nshafts of Bhimasena. Some amongst them, huge as hills, afflicted with\nfear and vomiting blood, ran away, their limbs mangled with arrows, and\nlooked on that account, like mountains with liquid metals running down\ntheir sides. People then beheld the two arms of Bhima, resembling two\nmighty snakes, smeared with sandal-paste and other pounded unguents,\ncontinually employed in drawing the bow. Hearing the sound of his\nbow-string and palms that resembled the peal of thunder, those elephants,\nejecting urine and excreta, ran away in fear. The feats of the\nsingle-handed Bhima of great intelligence, on that occasion, shone like\nthose of Rudra, himself, while engaged in destroying all creatures.'\"\n\n62"

  "passage_text": "\"Sanjaya said, 'The handsome Arjuna then, on that foremost car of his,\nunto which were yoked white steeds, and which was urged by Narayana\nhimself, appeared on the scene. Like the tempest agitating the ocean,\nVijaya, O foremost of kings, in that battle, agitated that host of thine\nteeming with horsemen. When the white-steeded Arjuna was otherwise\nengaged, thy son Duryodhana, filled with rage and surrounded by half his\ntroops, approached suddenly, and encompassed the advancing Yudhishthira\ninspired with the desire of revenge. The Kuru king then pierced the son\nof Pandu with three and seventy razor-headed arrows. At this,\nYudhishthira, the son of Kunti, became inflamed with ire, and quickly\nstruck thy son with thirty broad-headed arrows. The Kaurava troops then\nrushed impetuously for seizing Yudhishthira. Understanding the wicked\nintentions of the enemy, the great car-warriors of the Pandava army,\nuniting together, rushed towards Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, for\nrescuing him. Indeed, Nakula and Sahadeva and Dhrishtadyumna, the son of\nPrishata, surrounded by a full Akshauhini of troops, thus proceeded\ntowards Yudhishthira. Bhimasena also, in that battle, crushing the great\ncar-warriors of thy army, proceeded towards the king surrounded by foes.\nKarna, otherwise called Vaikartana, O king, shooting dense showers of\narrows, checked, single-handed, all those mighty bowmen thus advancing\n(to the rescue). Though they shot dense showers of arrows and hurled\ninnumerable lances, fighting with determination, yet they were unable\neven to look at the son of Radha. Indeed, the son of Radha, that master\nof all weapons offensive and defensive, by shooting dense showers of\nshafts checked all those great bowmen. The high-souled Sahadeva, however,\nquickly approaching (the spot where Duryodhana was), and invoking without\nloss of time a (celestial) weapon, pierced Duryodhana with twenty arrows.\nThus pierced by Sahadeva, the Kuru king, covered with blood, looked\nbeautiful, like a huge elephant of split temples. Seeing Duryodhana reduced to that plight, Karna, invoking his\nweapons quickly, began to slaughter the troops of Yudhishthira and\nPrishata's son. In\nconsequence then of the darkness caused by those showers of arrows, the\nbattle became awful to look at. Loud cries of woe arose from among thy\ntroops, O monarch, whilst they were being slaughtered by Dharma's son, O\nsire, with diverse kinds of keen shafts equipped with Kanka feathers and\nwhetted on stone, with numerous broad-headed arrows, and with diverse\nkinds of darts and swords and clubs. Thither where Pandu's son of\nvirtuous soul cast his eyes with the desire of producing evil, thither\nthy army broke, O bull of Bharata's race. Inflamed with great rage, Karna\nalso, of immeasurable soul, inspired with the desire of retaliating, his\nface flushed in anger, rushed in that battle against Pandu's son, king\nYudhishthira the just, shooting cloth-yard shafts and crescent-shaped\narrows and those equipped with heads like the calf's tooth. Yudhishthira\nalso pierced him with many whetted arrows equipped with wings of gold. As\nif smiling the while, Karna pierced the royal son of Pandu in the chest\nwith three broad-headed arrows, whetted on stone, and equipped with Kanka\nfeathers. Deeply afflicted therewith, king Yudhishthira the just, sitting\ndown on the terrace of his car, ordered his driver to retreat. Thereupon\nall the Dhartarashtras, with their king, set up a loud shout, saying,\n\"Seize! Seize!\" and all of them then pursued the (Pandava) king. Then\nseventeen hundred Kekaya troops, skilled in smiting, united with a body\nof the Pancala troops, O king, checked the Dhartarashtras. During the\nprogress of that fierce and terrible battle, Duryodhana and Bhima, those\ntwo warriors endued with great might, encountered each other.'\"\n\n63"

him in that battle. Beholding the son of Radha to be irresistible in that
battle, those warriors, afflicted with the arrows of their assailant,
repaired to the presence of Bhimasena. Breaking that car-force into many
parts by means of his arrows, Karna, singly and riding on that same car
of his, pursued Yudhishthira, who then, exceedingly mangled with arrows
and almost insensible, was proceeding slowly for reaching the Pandava
encampment with Nakula and Sahadeva on his two sides. Having approached
the king, the Suta's son, from desire of doing good to Duryodhana,
pierced the son of Pandu with three formidable arrows. In return, the
king pierced Radha's son in the centre of the chest and then his driver
with three shafts. Then those two scorchers of foes, viz., the twin sons
of Madri, those two protectors of Yudhishthira's car-wheels, rushed
towards Karna so that the latter might not succeed in slaying the king.
Then Nakula and Sahadeva, both shooting showers of shafts with great
care, covered the son of Radha therewith. The valiant son of the Suta,
however, in return, pierced those two high-souled chastisers of foes with
two broad-headed arrows of great sharpness. The son of Radha then slew
Yudhishthira's excellent steeds, white as ivory and fleet as the mind,
and having black hair in their tails. Then, smiling the while, the Suta's
son, that great bowman, with another broadheaded shaft, felled the
head-gear of Kunti's son. Similarly, the valiant Karna, having slain the
steeds of Nakula, cut off the car shafts and bow of that intelligent son
of Madri. Those two steedless and carless sons of Pandu,--those two
brothers,--thereupon ascended the car of Sahadeva. Beholding those two
brothers made carless, that slayer of hostile heroes, viz., their
maternal uncle, the ruler of the Madras, moved by compassion, addressed
the son of Radha and said, "Thou art to fight today with Pritha's son
Phalguna. Why dost thou then, with rage inflamed to such a pitch, battle
with Dharma's royal son? Thou art suffering thy weapons to be exhausted.
Thy own armour is being weakened. With thy shafts reduced, and without
quivers, with thy driver and steeds fatigued, and thyself mangled by foes
with weapons, when thou wilt approach Partha, O son of Radha, thou wilt
be an object of derision and mirth." Though thus addressed by the ruler
of the Madras, Karna still, filled with rage, continued to assail
Yudhishthira in battle. And he continued to pierce the two sons of Madri
by Pandu with many keen arrows. Smiling the while, by means of his shafts
he made Yudhishthira turn his face from the battle. Then Shalya,
laughing, once more said unto Karna as the latter, excited with great
wrath and resolved upon Yudhishthira's destruction stood on his car,
these words, "Him for whose sake Dhritarashtra's son always honours thee,
slay that Partha, O son of Radha. What wouldst thou gain by slaying
Yudhishthira? The two Krishnas are blowing their conchs, whose loud blare
is being heard. The twang also of Arjuna's bow is being heard, like the
roar of the clouds in the season of rains. There, Arjuna, striking down
the foremost of our car-warriors with his arrowy down-pours, is devouring
all our troops. Behold him, O Karna, in this battle. The two that are
protecting his rear are Yudhamanyu and Uttamauja. The brave Satyaki is
protecting his left wheel, and Dhrishtadyumna is protecting his right
wheel. There, Bhimasena is fighting with the royal son of Dhritarashtra.
Act in such way, O son of Radha, that Bhima may not be able to slay the
king today in the sight of us all,--that the king may, indeed, escape
him. Behold, Duryodhana is brought under the power of Bhimasena, that
ornament of battle. Approaching if thou canst rescue him, it will,
indeed, be a very wonderful feat. Going thither, rescue the king, for a
great peril has overtaken him. What wilt thou gain by slaying the sons of
Madri or king Yudhishthira?" Hearing these words of Shalya, O lord of
Earth, and beholding Duryodhana overpowered by Bhima in that dreadful
battle, the valiant son of Radha, thus urged by the words of Shalya and
exceedingly desirous of rescuing the king, left Ajatasatru and the twin
sons of Madri by Pandu, and rushed for rescuing thy son. He was borne by
his steeds that were fleet as birds and that were urged by the ruler of
the Madras. After Karna had gone away, Kunti's son Yudhishthira
retreated, borne, O sire, by the fleet steeds of Sahadeva. With his twin
brothers accompanying him, that ruler of men, quickly repairing in shame
to the (Pandava) camp, his body exceedingly mangled with shafts, alighted
from the car and hastily sat down on an excellent bed. The arrows then
being extracted from his body, the royal son of Pandu, his heart
exceedingly afflicted with sorrow's dart, addressed his two brothers,
viz., those two mighty car-warriors, the sons of Madri, saying, "Repair
quickly to the division of Bhimasena. Roaring like a cloud, Vrikodara is
engaged in battle." Riding another car, Nakula, that bull among
car-warriors, and Sahadeva of great energy,--those two brothers, those
two crushers of foes,--both endued with great might, then proceeded
towards Bhima, borne by steeds of the utmost fleetness. Indeed, the
brothers having together repaired to Bhimasena's division, took up their
places there.'"

64"

  "passage_text": ""Sanjaya said, 'Meanwhile Drona's son, surrounded by a large car-force, O
king, suddenly proceeded to that spot where Partha was. Like the
continent withstanding the surging ocean, the heroic Partha having Saurin
(Krishna) for his help-mate withstood the impetuously rushing
Ashvatthama. Then, O monarch, the valiant son of Drona, filled with rage,
covered both Arjuna and Vasudeva with his shafts. Beholding the two
Krishnas shrouded with arrows, the great car-warriors (of the Pandava
army), as also the Kurus that witnessed it, wondered exceedingly. Then
Arjuna, as if smiling, invoked into existence a celestial weapon. The
Brahmana Ashvatthama, however, O Bharata, baffled that weapon in that
battle. Indeed, all those weapons that Arjuna sped from desire of slaying
the son of Drona were baffled by the latter, that great bowman, in that
encounter. During the progress of that awful encounter of weapons, O
king, we beheld the son of Drona to resemble the Destroyer himself, with
gaping mouth. Having covered all the points of the compass, cardinal and
subsidiary, with straight arrows, he pierced Vasudeva with three arrows
in the right arm. Then Arjuna, slaying all the steeds of his high-souled
assailant, caused the Earth in that battle to be covered with a river of
blood that was exceedingly awful that led towards the other world, and
that had diverse kinds of creatures floating on it. All the spectators
beheld a large number of car-warriors along with their cars, belonging to
the division of Ashvatthama, slain and destroyed by means of the arrows
sped from Partha's bow. Ashvatthama also, slaying his enemies, caused a
terrible river of blood to flow there that led to Yama's domains. During
the progress of that fierce and awful battle between Drona's son and
Partha, the combatants fought without showing any regard for one another,
and rushed hither and thither. In consequence of cars having their steeds
and drivers slain, and steeds having their riders slain, and elephants
having their riders and guides slain, an awful carnage, O king, was made
by Partha in that battle! Car-warriors, deprived of life with shafts sped
from Partha's bow, fell down. Steeds freed from their trappings ran
hither and thither. Beholding those feats of Partha, that ornament of
battle, that valiant son of Drona quickly approached the former, that
foremost of victorious men, shook his formidable bow decked with gold,
and then pierced him from every side with many sharp arrows. Once more
bending the bow, O king, the son of Drona cruelly struck Arjuna, aiming
at the chest, with a winged arrow. Deeply pierced by Drona's son, O
Bharata, in that encounter, the wielder of Gandiva, that hero of great
intelligence forcibly covered the son of Drona with showers of arrows,
and then cut off his bow. His bow cut off Drona's son then, taking up a
spiked mace whose touch resembled that of thunder's, hurled it, in that
encounter, at the diadem-decked Arjuna. The son of Pandu, however, O
king, as if smiling the while, suddenly cut off that spiked mace decked
with gold, as it advanced towards him. Thus cut off with Partha's shafts,
it fell down on the Earth, like a mountain, O king, broken into pieces,
struck with the thunderbolt. Filled with rage at this, Drona's son, that
great car-warrior, began to cover Vibhatsu, aided by the energy of the
Aindra weapon. Beholding that shower of arrows spread over the welkin
through the Aindra weapon, Partha, endued with great activity, O king,
taking up his bow Gandiva, and fixing on his bowstring a mighty weapon
created by Indra, destroyed that Aindra-shower of arrows. Having baffled
that arrowy shower caused by the Aindra weapon, Partha soon covered the
car of Drona's son (with his own arrows). The son of Drona, however,
overwhelmed with Partha's shafts, penetrated through that shower of
arrows shot by the son of Pandu, and approaching the latter, invoked a
mighty weapon and suddenly pierced Krishna with hundred shafts and Arjuna
with three hundred small arrows. Then Arjuna pierced the son of his
preceptor with a hundred arrows in all his vital limbs. And then he
poured many arrows on the steeds and driver and the bowstring of Drona's
son in the very sight of thy warriors. Having pierced Drona's son in
every vital part, Pandu's son, that slayer of hostile heroes, then felled
his adversary's driver from the car-niche with a broad-headed arrow.
Drona's son, however, himself taking up the reins, covered Krishna with
many arrows. The activity of prowess that we then beheld in Drona's son
was exceedingly wonderful, since he guided his steeds while he fought
with Phalguni. That feat of his in battle, O king, was applauded by all
the warriors. Then Vibhatsu, otherwise called Jaya, smiling the while,
quickly cut off the traces of Ashvatthama's steeds in that battle, with a
razor-faced arrow. Already afflicted by the energy of Arjuna's shafts,
the steeds of Drona's son thereupon ran away. Then a loud noise arose
from thy troops, O Bharata! Meanwhile the Pandavas, having obtained the
victory, and desiring to improve it, rushed against thy troops, shooting
from all sides sharp arrows at them. The vast Dhartarashtra host, then, O
king, was repeatedly broken by the heroic Pandavas inspired with desire
of victory, in the very sight, O monarch, of thy sons, conversant with
all modes of warfare, and of Shakuni the son of Subala, and of Karna, O
king! Though sought to be stopped, O king, by thy sons, that great army,
afflicted on all sides, stayed not on the field. Indeed, a confusion set
in among the vast terrified host of thy son in consequence of many
warriors flying away on all sides. The Suta's son loudly cried out,
saying "Stay, Stay!" but thy army, slaughtered by many high-souled
warriors, did not stay on the field. Loud shouts were uttered then, O
monarch, by the Pandavas, inspired with this desire of victory, on
beholding the Dhartarashtra host flying away on all sides. Then"

  "passage_text": "\"Sanjaya said, 'Having vanquished the son of Drona and achieved a mighty\nand heroic feat that is exceedingly difficult of accomplishment,\nDhananjaya, irresistible by foes, and with bow outstretched in his hands,\ncast his eyes among his own troops. The brave Savyasaci, gladdening those\nwarriors of his that were still battling at the head of their divisions\nand applauding those among them that were celebrated for their former\nachievements, caused the car-warriors of his own army to continue to stand\nin their posts. Not seeing his brother Yudhishthira of Ajamida's race,\nthe diadem-decked Arjuna, adorned, besides, with a necklace of gold,\nspeedily approached Bhima and enquired of him the whereabouts of the\nking, saying, \"Tell me, where is the king?\" Thus asked, Bhima said, \"King\nYudhishthira the just, hath gone away from this place, his limbs scorched\nwith Karna's shafts. It is doubtful whether he still liveth!\" Hearing\nthose words, Arjuna said, \"For this reason go thou quickly from the spot\nfor bringing intelligence of the king, that best of all the descendants\nof Kuru! Without doubt, deeply pierced by Karna with shafts, the king\nhath gone to the camp! In that fierce passage at arms, though deeply\npierced by Drona with keen shafts, the king endued with great activity,\nhad still stayed in battle, expectant of victory, until Drona was slain!\nThat foremost one among the Pandavas, possessed of great magnanimity, was\ngreatly imperilled by Karna in today's battle! I will stay here, checking all our\nfoes!\" Thus addressed, Bhima said, \"O thou of great glory, go thyself for\nascertaining the condition of the king, that bull amongst the Bharatas!\nIf, O Arjuna, I go there, many foremost of heroes will then say that I am\nfrightened in battle!\" Then Arjuna said unto Bhimasena, \"The samsaptakas\nare before my division! Without slaying those assembled foes first, it is\nimpossible for me to stir from this place!\" Then Bhimasena said unto\nArjuna, \"Relying upon my own might, O foremost one among the Kurus, I\nwill fight with all the samsaptakas in battle! Therefore, O Dhananjaya,\ndo thou go thyself!\"'\"\n\n\"Sanjaya continued, 'Hearing in the midst of foes, those words of his\nbrother Bhimasena that were difficult of accomplishment, Arjuna, desiring\nto see the king, addressed the Vrishni hero, saying, \"Urge the steeds, O\nHrishikesha, leaving this sea of troops! I desire, O Keshava to see king\nAjatasatru!\"'\"\n\n\"Sanjaya continued, 'Just as he was on the point of urging the steeds,\nKeshava, that foremost one of the Dasharhas, addressed Bhima, saying,\n\"This feat is not at all wonderful for thee, O Bhima! I am about to go\n(hence). Slay these assembled foes of Partha!\" Then Hrishikesha proceeded\nwith very great speed to the spot where king Yudhishthira was, O king,\nborne by those steeds that resembled Garuda, having stationed Bhima, that\nchastiser of foes, at the head of the army and having commanded him, O\nmonarch, to fight (with the samsaptakas). Then those two foremost of men,\n(Krishna and Arjuna), proceeding on their car, approached the king who\nwas lying alone on his bed. Both of them, alighting from that car,\nworshipped the feet of king Yudhishthira the just. Beholding that bull of\ntigers among men safe and sound, the two Krishnas became filled with joy,\nlike the twin Ashvinis on seeing Vasava. The king then congratulated them\nboth like Vivasvat congratulating the twin Ashvinis, or like Brihaspati\ncongratulating Sankara and Vishnu after the slaughter of the mighty asura\nJambha. King Yudhishthira the just, thinking that Karna had been slain,\nbecame filled with joy, and that scorcher of foes thereupon addressed\nthem in these words in a voice choked with delight.'\"\n\n66"

  "passage_text": ""'Yudhishthira said, "Welcome, O thou that hast Devaki for thy mother,
and welcome to thee, O Dhananjaya! The sight of both of you, O Acyuta and
Arjuna, is exceedingly agreeable! I see that without being wounded
yourselves, you two, his foes, have slain the mighty car-warrior Karna!
He was in battle like unto a snake of virulent poison. He was
accomplished in all weapons. The leader of all the Dhartarashtras, he was
their armour and protector! While fighting he was always protected by
Vrishasena and by Sushena, both of whom are great bowmen! Of great
energy, he had received lessons from Rama in weapons! He was invincible
in battle! The foremost one in all the world, as a car-warrior he was
celebrated throughout all the worlds. He was the saviour of the
Dhartarashtras, and the proceeder in their van! A slayer of hostile
troops, he was the crusher of large bands of foes. Ever engaged in
Duryodhana's good, he was always prepared to inflict woe on us! He was
invincible in battle by the very gods with Vasava at their head. In
energy and might he was equal unto the god of fire and the god of wind.
In gravity he was unfathomable as the Nether world. The enhancer of the
joys of friends, he was like the Destroyer himself unto foes! Having
slain Karna (who was even so) in dreadful battle, by good luck it is that
you two have come, like a couple of celestials after vanquishing an
Asura! Today, O Acyuta and Arjuna, a great battle was fought between
myself exerting with might and that hero resembling the Destroyer
himself, while seeking to exterminate all creatures! My standard was cut
down, and my two Parshni drivers also were slain by him. I was also made
steedless and carless by him in the very sight of Yuyudhana, of
Dhrishtadyumna, of the twins (Nakula and Sahadeva), of the heroic
Shikhandi, as also in the very sight of the sons of Draupadi, and all the
Pancalas! Having vanquished those innumerable foes, Karna of mighty
energy then vanquished me, O thou of mighty arms, although I exerted
myself resolutely in battle! Pursuing me then and without doubt,
vanquishing all my protectors, that foremost of warriors addressed me in
diverse harsh speeches. That I am still alive, O Dhananjaya, is due to
the prowess of Bhimasena. What more need I say? I am unable to bear that
humiliation! For thirteen years, O Dhananjaya, through fear of Karna, I
did not obtain any sleep by night or any comfort by day! Filled with
hatred of Karna, I burn, O Dhananjaya! Like the bird Vaddhrinasa I fled
from Karna, knowing that the time for my own destruction had come. The
whole of my time had passed in the thought as to how I would accomplish
the destruction of Karna in battle! Awake or asleep, O son of Kunti, I
always beheld Karna (with my mind's eye). Wherever I was, the universe
appeared to me to be full of Karna! Inspired with the fear of Karna,
wherever I used to go, O Dhananjaya, thither I beheld Karna standing
before my eyes! Vanquished in battle, with my steeds and car, by that
hero who never retreated from battle, alive I was let off by him! What
use have I of life or of kingdom either, since Karna, that ornament of
battle, today cried fie on me? That which I had never before met with at
the hands of Bhishma or Kripa or Drona in battle, that I met with today
at the hands of the Suta's son, that mighty car-warrior! It is for this,
O son of Kunti, that I ask thee today about thy welfare! Tell me in
detail how thou hast slain Karna today! In battle Karna was equal unto
Sakra himself. In prowess he was equal unto Yama. In weapons he was equal
unto Rama. How then hath he been slain? He was regarded as a mighty
car-warrior, conversant with all modes of warfare. He was the foremost of
all bowmen, and the one man amongst all men! O prince, the son of Radha
was always worshipped by Dhritarashtra and his son, for thy sake! How
then hath he been slain by thee? In all engagements, Dhritarashtra's son,
O Arjuna, used to regard Karna as thy death, O bull among men! How then,
O tiger among men, hath that Karna been slain by thee in battle? Tell me,
O son of Kunti, how that Karna hath been slain by thee! How, while he was
engaged in battle, didst thou, O tiger among men, strike off his head in
the very sight of all his friends like a tiger tearing off the head of a
ruru deer? That Suta's son who in battle searched all the points of the
compass for finding thee, that Karna who had promised to give a car with
six bulls of elephantine proportions unto him that would point thee out,
I ask: doth that Karna of wicked soul lie today on the bare ground, slain
with thy keen arrows equipped with Kanka feathers? Having slain the
Suta's son in battle, thou hast accomplished a deed highly agreeable to
me! Encountering him in battle, hast thou really slain that Suta's son,
who, filled with arrogance and pride and bragging of his heroism, used to
search everywhere on the field of battle for thee? Hast thou, O sire,
really slain in battle that sinful wretch who used to always challenge
thee and who was desirous for thy sake of giving unto others a
magnificent car, made of gold along with a number of elephants and bulls
and steeds? Hast thou really slain today that sinful wight who was
exceedingly dear to Suyodhana, and who, intoxicated with pride of
heroism, used always to brag in the assembly of the Kurus? Encountered in
battle, doth that wretch lie today on the field, his limbs exceedingly
mangled with sky-ranging shafts sped by thee from thy bow and all steeped
in blood? Have the two arms of Dhritarashtra's son been (at last) broken?
Have those words been unfulfilled, uttered from folly by him who, filled
with pride, used to always boast in the midst of the kings for gladdening
Duryodhana, saying, 'I will slay Phalguna'? O son of Indra, hath that
Karna of little understanding been slain by thee today, that Suta's son
who made the vow that he would not wash his feet as long as Partha lived?"
}

That Karna who had vowed for thy sake, saying that he would not\nreturn from battle without having slain Krishna and Partha. I ask, doth\nthat Karna of sinful understanding lie today on the field, his body\npierced with shafts? Thou knowest the nature of the battle that took\nplace when the Srinjayas and the Kauravas encountered each other, the\nbattle in which I was brought to that distressful plight. O Savyasaci, hast thou today, with\nblazing shafts sped from Gandiva, cut off from the trunk of that Karna of\nwicked understanding his resplendent head decked with earrings? That\nSuta's son of wicked soul, that Karna of great wrath, who had formerly,\nin the presence of the Kauravas and in the midst of the assembly called\nus sesame seeds without kernel, encountering that Karna in battle, hast\nthou slain him today? That Suta's son of wicked soul who had, laughing\nthe while, commanded Duhshasana to forcibly drag Yajnasena's daughter won\nin gambling by Subala's son, hath he been slain today by thee? That Karna\nof little understanding who, having been counted as only half a\ncar-warrior during the tale of rathas and atirathas, had upbraided that\nforemost of all wielders of weapons on Earth, our grandsire Bhishma, hath\nhe been slain by thee? Extinguish, O Phalguna, this fire in my heart that\nis born of vindictiveness and is fanned by the wind of humiliation, by\ntelling me that thou hast slain Karna today, having encountered him in\nbattle! The news of Karna's slaughter is exceedingly agreeable to me.\nTell me, therefore, how the Suta's son hath been slain! Like the divine\nVishnu waiting for the arrival of Indra with the intelligence of Vritra's\nslaughter, I had so long waited for thee, O hero!\"'\"\n\n67"
}

Beholding my car, of\nrattle deep as the roar of clouds, all the troops began to encompass it.\nSlaying full five hundred of those, I then, O foremost of kings,\nproceeded against Drona's son. Approaching me, O king, that hero with\ngreat resolution rushed against me like a prince of elephants against a\nlion, and desired to rescue, O monarch, the Kaurava car-warriors that\nwere being slaughtered by me. While engaged in battle with me, eight\ncarts, each drawn by eight bullocks, carried his hundreds of arrows. He\nshot them all at me, but like a wind destroying the clouds I destroyed\nwith my shafts that arrowy shower of his. He then shot at me, with skill\nand force and resolution, thousands of other arrows, all sped from his\nbow-string stretched to his very ear, even like a black cloud in the\nseason of rains pouring in torrents the water with which it is charged.\nSo quickly did Drona's son career in that battle that we could not\ndiscern from which side, the left or the right, he shot his arrows, nor\ncould we notice when he took up his arrows and when he let them off.\nIndeed, the bow of Drona's son was seen by us to be incessantly drawn to\na circle. At last, the son of Drona pierced me with five whetted arrows\nand Vasudeva also with five whetted arrows. Within the twinkling of an\neye, however, I afflicted him with the force of thunderbolts. Exceedingly\nafflicted with those shafts sped by me, he soon assumed the form of a\nporcupine. All his limbs became bathed in blood. Beholding his troops,\nthose foremost of warriors all covered with blood and overwhelmed by me,\nhe then entered the car-division of the Suta's son. Seeing the troops\noverwhelmed by me in battle, and struck with fear, and beholding the\nelephants and steeds flying away, that grinder (of hostile hosts), viz.,\nKarna approached me quickly with fifty great car-warriors. Slaying them\nall and avoiding Karna, I have quickly come hither for seeing thee. All\nthe Pancalas are afflicted with fear at sight of Karna like kine at the\nscent of a lion. The Prabhadrakas also, O king, having approached Karna,\nare like persons that have entered the wide open jaws of Death. Karna has\nalready despatched to Yama's abode full seventeen hundred of those\ndistressed car-warriors. Indeed, O king, the Suta's son did not become\ncheerless till he had a sight of us. Thou hadst first been engaged with\nAshvatthama and exceedingly mangled by him. I heard that after that thou\nwert seen by Karna. O thou of inconceivable feats, I thought that thou\nmust have, O king, been enjoying rest (in the camp), having come away\nfrom the cruel Karna. I have seen, O son of Pandu, the great and\nwonderful (Bhargava) weapon of Karna displayed in the van of battle.\nThere is now no other warrior among the Srinjayas that is able to resist\nthe mighty car-warrior Karna. Let Sini's grandson Satyaki and\nDhrishtadyumna, O king, be the protectors of my car-wheels. Let the\nheroic princes Yudhamanyu and Uttamauja protect my rear. O thou of great\nglory, encountering that heroic and invincible car-warrior, viz., the\nSuta's son, staying in the hostile army, like Sakra encountering Vritra,\nO foremost of kings, I will, O Bharata, fight with the Suta's son if he\ncan be found in this battle today. Come and behold me and the Suta's son\ncontending with each other in battle for victory. There, the Prabhadrakas\nare rushing towards the face of a mighty bull. There, O Bharata, 6,000\nprinces are sacrificing themselves in battle today, for the sake of\nheaven. If, putting forth my strength, I do not, O king, slay Karna today\nwith all his relatives while engaged in battle with him, then that end\nwill be mine, O lion among kings, which is his that does not accomplish a\nvow taken by him. I beg of thee, bless me, saying that victory will be\nmine in battle. Yonder, the Dhartarashtras are about to devour Bhima. I\nwill, O lion among kings, slay the Suta's son and his troops and all our\nfoes!\"'\"\n\n68"

  "passage_text": "\"Sanjaya said, 'Hearing that Karna of mighty energy was still alive,\nPritha's son Yudhishthira of immeasurable energy, exceedingly angry with\nPhalguna and burning with the shafts of Karna, said these words unto\nDhananjaya, \"O sire, thy army is fled and hath been beaten in a way that\nis scarcely honourable! Inspired with fear and deserting Bhima, thou hast\ncome hither since thou hast been unable to slay Karna. Thou hast, by\nentering her womb, rendered the conception of Kunti abortive. Thou hast\nacted improperly by deserting Bhima, because thou wert unable to slay the\nSuta's son. Thou hadst, O Partha, said unto me in the Dwaita woods that\nthou wouldst, on a single car, slay Karna. Why, then, through fear of\nKarna hast come hither, avoiding Karna and deserting Bhima? If in the\nDwaita woods thou hadst said unto me, 'O king, I shall not be able to\nfight with Karna,' we would then, O Partha, have made other arrangements\nsuitable to the circumstances. Having promised me the slaughter of Karna,\nthou hast not, O hero, kept that promise. Bringing us into the midst of\nfoes, why hast thou broken us into pieces by throwing us down on a hard\nsoil? Expecting diverse good things and benefits from thee, O Arjuna, we\nhave always uttered blessings on thee. All those expectations, however, O\nprince, have proved vain like those of persons expectant of fruit getting\ninstead of a tree burthened only with flowers! Like a fish-hook hid\nwithin a piece of meat, or poison overlaid with food, thou didst, for\ndisappointing us at last, point out destruction in the shape of kingdom\nunto ourselves covetous of kingdom! For these thirteen years, O\nDhananjaya, we have, from hope, lived relying on thee, like seeds sown on\nearth in expectation of the showers sent by the gods in season! Even\nthese were the words that a voice in the skies had said unto Pritha on\nthe seventh day after thy birth, O thou of foolish understanding! 'This\nson of thine that is born will have the prowess of Vasava himself! He\nwill vanquish all his heroic foes! Endued with superior energy, he will\nat Khandava vanquish all the celestials united together and diverse other\ncreatures. This one will subjugate the Madras, the Kalingas, and the\nKaikeyas. This one will, in the midst of many kings, slay the Kurus.\nThere will be no bowman superior to him, and no creature will ever be\nable to vanquish him. With his senses under control, and having obtained\nmastery over all branches of knowledge, this one, by merely desiring it,\nwill bring all creatures under subjection to himself. This high-souled\nson that is born of thee, O Kunti, will in beauty be the rival of Soma,\nin speed of the god of wind, in patience of Meru, in forgiveness of\nEarth, in splendour of Surya, in prosperity of the Lord of treasures, in\ncourage of Sakra, and in might of Vishnu. He will be the slayer of all\nfoes like Vishnu, the son of Aditi. Endued with immeasurable energy, he\nwill be celebrated for the destruction he will deal to foes and the\nsuccess he will win for friends. He will, besides, be the founder of a\nrace!' Even thus, in the skies, on the summit of the Satasringa\nmountains, in the hearing of many ascetics, that voice spoke. All that,\nhowever, hath not come to pass. Alas, it shows that the gods even may\nspeak untruths! Hearing also the words of praise always uttered about\nthee by many foremost of Rishis, I never expected that Suyodhana would\nwin success and prosperity or that thou thyself wouldst be afflicted with\nthe fear of Karna! Thou ridest upon an excellent car constructed by the\ncelestial artificer himself, with axles that do not creak, and with\nstandard that bears the ape. Thou bearest a sword attached to thy belt of\ngold and silk. This thy bow Gandiva is full six cubits long. Thou hast\nKeshava for thy driver. Why, then, through fear of Karna hast thou come\naway from battle, O Partha? If, O thou of wicked soul, thou hadst given\nthis bow to Keshava and become his driver, then Keshava could have (by\nthis time) slain the fierce Karna like the lord of the Maruts (Sakra)\nslaying with his thunder the Asura Vritra. If thou art unable to resist\nthe fierce son of Radha today, as he is careering in battle, give this\nthy Gandiva today to some other king, that may be thy superior in (the\nuse and knowledge of) weapons. If that be done, the world will not then\nbehold us bereft of sons and wives, deprived of happiness in consequence\nof the loss of kingdom, and sunk, O son of Pandu, in an unfathomable hell\nof great misery. It would have been better for thee if thou hadst never\nbeen born in the womb of Kunti, or having taken thy birth there, if thou\nhadst come out on the fifth month an abortion, than to have, O prince,\nthus come away from battle, O thou of wicked soul! Fie on thy Gandiva,\nfie on the might of thy arms, fie on thy inexhaustible arrows! Fie on thy\nbanner with the gigantic ape on it, and fie on thy car given thee by the\ngod of fire!\"'\"\n\n69"

  "passage_text": ""Sanjaya said, 'Thus addressed by Yudhishthira, Kunti's son owning white
steeds, filled with rage, drew his sword for slaying that bull of
Bharata's race. Beholding his wrath, Keshava, conversant with the
workings of the (human) heart said, "Why, O Partha, dost thou draw thy
sword? I do not, O Dhananjaya, behold anyone here with whom thou hast to
fight! The Dhartarashtras have now been assailed by the intelligent
Bhimasena. Thou comest from battle, O son of Kunti, for seeing the king.
The king has been seen by thee. Indeed, Yudhishthira is well. Having seen
that tiger among kings who is endued with prowess equal to that of a
tiger, why this folly at a time when thou shouldst rejoice? I do not see
here, O son of Kunti, the person whom thou mayst slay. Why then dost thou
desire to strike? What is this delusion of thy mind? Why dost thou, with
such speed, take up that formidable sword? I ask thee this, O son of
Kunti! What is this that thou art about, inasmuch as, O thou of
inconceivable prowess, thou graspest that sword in anger?" Thus addressed
by Krishna, Arjuna, casting his eyes on Yudhishthira, and breathing like
an angry snake, said unto Govinda, "I would cut off the head of that man
who would tell me 'Give thy Gandiva to another person.' Even this is my
secret vow. Those words have been spoken by this king, O thou of
immeasurable prowess, in thy presence, O Govinda! I dare not forgive
them. I will for that slay this king who himself fears the slightest
falling from virtue. Slaying this best of men, I will keep my vow. It is
for this that I have drawn the sword, O delighter of the Yadus. Even I,
slaying Yudhishthira, will pay off my debt to truth. By that I will
dispel my grief and fever, O Janardana. I ask thee, what do you think
suitable to the circumstances that have arisen? Thou, O sire, knowest the
entire past and future of this universe. I will do what thou wilt tell
me."'"

"Sanjaya continued, 'Govinda then said, "Fie, fie," unto Partha and once
more continued to say, "I now know, O Partha, that thou hast not waited
upon the old, since, O tiger among men, thou hast yielded to wrath at a
time when thou shouldst not have done so. No one that is acquainted with
the distinctions of morality would act in the way, O Dhananjaya, in which
thou, O son of Pandu, that art unacquainted with them, art acting today!
He, O Partha, is the worst of men who committeth acts that should not be
done and doeth acts that are apparently proper but condemned by the
scriptures. Thou knowest not the decisions of those learned men who,
waited upon by pupils, declare their opinions, following the dictates of
morality. The man that is not acquainted with those rulings becomes
confounded and stupefied, O Partha, even as thou hast been stupefied, in
discriminating between what should be done and what should not. What
should be done and what should not cannot be ascertained easily.
Everything can be ascertained by the aid of the scriptures. Thou,
however, art not acquainted with the scriptures. Since (believing
thyself) conversant with morality, thou art desirous of observing
morality (in this way, it seems) thou art actuated by ignorance. Thou
believest thyself to be conversant with virtue, but thou dost not know, O
Partha, that the slaughter of living creatures is a sin. Abstention from
injury to animals is, I think, the highest virtue. One may even speak an
untruth, but one should never kill. How then, O foremost of men, couldst
thou wish, like an ordinary person, to slay thy eldest brother, the King,
who is conversant with morality? The slaughter of a person not engaged in
battle, or of a foe, O Bharata who has turned his face from battle or who
flies away or seeks protection or joins his hands or yields himself up or
is carless, is never applauded by the righteous. All these attributes
are in thy superior. This vow, O Partha, was adopted by thee before from
foolishness. In consequence of that vow thou art now, from folly,
desirous of perpetrating a sinful act. Why, O Partha, dost thou rush
towards thy reverend superior for slaying him, without having resolved
the exceedingly subtle course of morality that is, again, difficult of
being understood? I will now tell thee, O son of Pandu, this mystery
connected with morality, this mystery that was declared by Bhishma, by
the righteous Yudhishthira, by Vidura otherwise called Kshatri, and by
Kunti, of great celebrity. I will tell thee that mystery in all its
details. Listen to it, O Dhananjaya! One who speaks truth is righteous.
There is nothing higher than truth. Behold, however, truth as practised
is exceedingly difficult to be understood as regards its essential
attributes. Truth may be unutterable, and even falsehood may be utterable
where falsehood would become truth and truth would become falsehood. In a
situation of peril to life and in marriage, falsehood becomes utterable.
In a situation involving the loss of one's entire property, falsehood
becomes utterable. On an occasion of marriage, or of enjoying a woman, or
when life is in danger, or when one's entire property is about to be
taken away, or for the sake of a Brahmana, falsehood may be uttered.
These five kinds of falsehood have been declared to be sinless. On these
occasions falsehood would become truth and truth would become falsehood.
He is a fool that practises truth without knowing the difference between
truth and falsehood. One is said to be conversant with morality when one
is able to distinguish between truth and falsehood. What wonder then in
this that a man of wisdom, by perpetrating even a cruel act, may obtain
great merit like Valaka by the slaughter of the blind beast? What wonder,
again, in this that a foolish and ignorant person, from even the desire
of winning merit, earns great sin like Kausika (living) among the rivers?"

"'Arjuna said, "Tell me, O holy one, this story that I may understand it,
viz., this illustration about Valaka and about Kausika (living) among
rivers.""

  "passage_text": "\"'Vasudeva said, \"There was a certain hunter of animals, O Bharata, of\nthe name of Valaka. He used, for the livelihood of his son and wives and\nnot from will, to slay animals. Devoted to the duties of his own order\nand always speaking the truth and never harbouring malice, he used also\nto support his parents and others that depended upon him. One day,\nsearching for animals even with perseverance and care, he found none. At\nlast he saw a beast of prey whose sense of smell supplied the defect of\nhis eyes, employed in drinking water. Although he had never seen such an\nanimal before, still he slew it immediately. After the slaughter of that\nblind beast, a floral shower fell from the skies (upon the head of the\nhunter). A celestial car also, exceedingly delightful and resounding with\nthe songs of Apsaras and the music of their instruments, came from heaven\nfor taking away that hunter of animals. That beast of prey, having\nundergone ascetic austerities, had obtained a boon and had become the\ncause of the destruction of all creatures. For this reason he was made\nblind by the Self-born. Having slain that animal which had resolved to\nslay all creatures, Valaka went to heaven. Morality is even so difficult\nof being understood. There was an ascetic of the name of Kausika without\nmuch knowledge of the scriptures. He lived in a spot much removed from a\nvillage, at a point where many rivers met. He made a vow, saying, 'I must\nalways speak the truth.' He then became celebrated, O Dhananjaya, as a\nspeaker of truth. At that time certain persons, from fear of robbers,\nentered that wood (where Kausika dwelt). Thither even, the robbers,\nfilled with rage, searched for them carefully. Approaching Kausika then,\nthat speaker of truth, they asked him saying, 'O holy one, by which path\nhave a multitude of men gone a little while before? Asked in the name of\nTruth, answer us. If thou hast seen them, tell us this'. Thus adjured,\nKausika told them the truth, saying, 'Those men have entered this wood\ncrowded with many trees and creepers and plants'. Even thus, O Partha,\ndid Kausika give them the information. Then those cruel men, it is heard,\nfinding out the persons they sought, slew them all. In consequence of\nthat great sin consisting in the words spoken, Kausika, ignorant of the\nsubtilities of morality, fell into a grievous hell, even as a foolish\nman, of little knowledge, and unacquainted with the distinctions of\nmorality, falleth into painful hell by not having asked persons of age\nfor the solution of his doubts. There must be some indications for\ndistinguishing virtue from sin. Sometimes that high and unattainable\nknowledge may be had by the exercise of reason. Many persons say, on the\none hand, that the scriptures indicate morality. I do not contradict\nthis. The scriptures, however, do not provide for every case. For the\ngrowth of creatures have precepts of morality been declared. That which\nis connected with inoffensiveness is religion. Dharma protects and\npreserves the people. So it is the conclusion of the Pandits that what\nmaintains is Dharma. O Partha, I have narrated to you the signs and\nindications of Dharma. Hearing this, you decide whether Yudhishthira is\nto be slaughtered by you or not.\" Arjuna said, \"Krishna, your words are\nfraught with great intelligence and impregnated with wisdom. Thou art to\nus like our parents and our refuge. Nothing is unknown to thee in the\nthree worlds, so thou art conversant with the canons of morality. O\nKeshava of the Vrishni clan, thou knowest my vow that whoever among men\nwould tell me, 'Partha, give thy Gandiva to some one braver than you,' I\nshall at once put an end to his life. Bhima has also made a promise that\nwhoever would call him 'tularak', would be slaughtered by him there and\nthen. Now the King has repeatedly used those very words to me in thy\npresence, O hero, viz., 'Give thy bow.' If I slay him, O Keshava, I will\nnot be able to live in this world for even a moment. Having intended\nagain the slaughter of the king through folly and the loss of my mental\nfaculties, I have been polluted by sin. It behoveth thee today, O\nforemost of all righteous persons, to give me such counsel that my vow,\nknown throughout the world, may become true while at the same time both\nmyself and the eldest son of Pandu may live.\"'\""
}

After\nthat, O hero, he was repeatedly struck by the Suta's son (with his\nshafts), while he was retreating from battle. Having afflicted his foes at the proper time in battle, and\nslain many brave lords of earth and many foremost of car-warriors and\nhuge elephants and many heroic horsemen and countless brave combatants,\nhe hath, in addition, slain a 1,000 elephants and 10,000 Kamboja\nmountaineers, and is uttering loud roars in battle like a lion after\nslaying innumerable smaller animals. What wouldst thou gain\nby always being obedient to a cruel person like me? A wretch that I am, I\nshall this very day retire into the woods. Live you happily without me.\nThe high-souled Bhimasena is fit to be king. A eunuch that I am, what\nshall I do with sovereignty? I am incapable of bearing these harsh\nspeeches of thee excited with wrath. Let Bhima become king. Having been\ninsulted thus, O hero, what use have I with life.\" Having said these\nwords, the king, leaving that bed, suddenly stood up and desired to go to\nthe woods. That man in the world who would tell\nhim, 'Give thy Gandiva to another', would be slain by him. Even those\nvery words were addressed to him by you. Having obtained thee, O Acyuta, we are not masterless.\"'\"\n\n71\n\n\"Sanjaya said, 'Having heard these joyful words of king Yudhishthira,\nGovinda of virtuous soul, that delighter of the Yadus, then addressed\nPartha. The latter, however, having at the instance of Krishna addressed\nthose words unto Yudhishthira, became exceedingly cheerless for having\ncommitted a trivial sin. Then Vasudeva, smiling, said unto the son of\nPandu, \"What would have been thy condition, O Partha, if, observant of\nvirtue thou hadst slain the son of Dharma with thy sharp sword? Thou wouldst have sunk also in terrible\nhell in consequence of the slaughter of thy brother. Gratify now this\nking of virtuous behaviour, this foremost of all practisers of virtue,\nthis chief of Kuru's race. Even this is my wish. Gratifying the king with\ndevotion, and after Yudhishthira will have been made happy, we two will\nproceed against the car of the Suta's son for fighting him. Slaying Karna\ntoday with thy keen shafts in battle, do thou, O giver of honours, give\ngreat happiness to Dharma's son. Even this, O mighty-armed one, is what I\nthink to be suitable to this hour. Having done this, thy purpose will be\nachieved.\" Then Arjuna, O monarch, in shame, touched king Yudhishthira's\nfeet with his head. And he repeatedly said unto that chief of the\nBharatas, \"Be pleased with me, Forgive, O king, all that I have said from\ndesire of observing virtue and from fear of sins.\"'\""

We have seen many heroes, who, endued with prowess like that\nSakra, have attained to the highest regions, encountering thy heroic self\nin battle! Who else, O puissant one, that is not equal to thee, would be\nsafe and sound after encountering Drona and Bhishma and Bhagadatta, O\nsire, and Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti and Sudakshina, the chief of the\nKambojas and Srutayudha of mighty energy and Acyutayudha as well? Thou\nhast celestial weapons, and lightness of hand and might, and thou art\nnever stupefied in battle! Thou hast also that humility which is due to\nknowledge! Thou canst strike with effect! Thou hast sureness of aim, and\npresence of mind as regards the selection of means, O Arjuna! Thou art\ncompetent to destroy all mobile and immobile creatures including the very\ngods with the Gandharvas! On earth, O Partha, there is no human warrior\nwho is equal to thee in battle. Amongst all Kshatriyas, invincible in\nbattle, that wield the bow, amongst the very gods, I have not seen or\nheard of even one that is equal to thee. The Creator of all beings, viz.,\nBrahma himself created the great bow Gandiva with which thou fightest, O\nPartha! For this reason there is no one that is equal to thee. I must,\nhowever, O son of Pandu, say that which is beneficial to thee. Do not, O\nmighty-armed one, disregard Karna, that ornament of battle! Karna is\npossessed of might. He is proud and accomplished in weapons. He is a\nmaharatha. He is accomplished (in the ways of battle) and conversant with\nall modes of warfare. He is also well-acquainted with all that suits\nplace and time. What need is there of saying much? Hear in brief, O son\nof Pandu! I regard the mighty car-warrior Karna as thy equal, or perhaps,\nthy superior! With the greatest care and resolution shouldst thou slay\nhim in great battle. In energy he is equal to Agni. As regards speed, he\nis equal to the impetuosity of the wind. In wrath, he resembles the\nDestroyer himself. Endued with might, he resembles a lion in the\nformation of his body. He is eight ratnis in stature. His arms are large.\nHis chest is broad. He is invincible. He is sensitive. He is a hero. He\nis, again, the foremost of heroes. He is exceedingly handsome. Possessed\nof every accomplishment of a warrior, he is a dispeller of the fears of\nfriends. Engaged in the good of Dhritarashtra's son, he always hates the\nsons of Pandu. No one, not even the gods with Vasava at their head, can\nslay the son of Radha, save thee, as I think. Slay, therefore, the Suta's\nson today. No one possessed of flesh and blood, not even the gods\nfighting with great care, not all the warriors (of the three worlds)\nfighting together can vanquish that car-warrior. Towards the Pandavas he\nis always of wicked soul and sinful behaviour, and cruel, and of wicked\nintelligence. In his quarrel with the sons of Pandu, he is actuated by no\nconsideration affecting his own interests. Slaying that Karna, therefore,\nfulfill thy purpose today. Despatch today unto Yama's presence that\nSuta's son, that foremost of car-warriors, whose death is near. Indeed,\nslaying that Suta's son, that first of car-warriors, show thy love for\nYudhishthira the just. I know thy prowess truly, O Partha, which is\nincapable of being resisted by the gods and Asuras. The Suta's son of\nwicked soul, from exceeding pride, always disregards the sons of Pandu. O\nDhananjaya, slay that man today for whose sake the wretched Duryodhana\nregardeth himself a hero, that root of all (those) sinful persons, that\nson of a Suta. Slay, O Dhananjaya, that tiger among men, that active and\nproud Karna, who hath a sword for his tongue, a bow for his mouth, and\narrows for his teeth. I know thee well as regards the energy and the\nmight that are in thee. Slay the brave Karna in battle, like a lion\nslaying an elephant. Slay in battle today, O Partha, that Karna,\notherwise called Vaikartana, in consequence of whose energy\nDhritarashtra's son disregards thine.\"'\"\n\n73"

unto Arjuna, who, O Bharata, was advancing (to battle), firmly resolved
upon slaying Karna, "Today is the seventeenth day, O Bharata, of this
terrible massacre of men and elephants and steeds. At the outset vast was
the host that belonged to you. Encountering the foe in battle, that host
has been very much reduced in numbers, O king! The Kauravas also, O
Partha, were numerous at first, teeming with elephants and steeds.
Encountering thee, however, as their foe, they have been nearly
exterminated in the van of battle! These lords of Earth and these
Srinjayas, united together, and these Pandava troops also, obtaining thy
invincible self as their leader, are maintaining their ground on the
field. Protected by thee, O slayer of foes, the Pancalas, the Matsyas,
the Karushas, and the Cedis, have caused a great destruction of thy foes.
Who is there that can vanquish the assembled Kauravas in battle? On the
other hand, who is there that can vanquish the mighty car-warriors of the
Pandavas protected by thee? Thou, however, art competent to vanquish in
battle the three worlds consisting of the gods, the Asuras, and human
beings, united together. What need I say then of the Kaurava host? Save
thee, O tiger among men, who else is there, even if he resemble Vasava
himself in prowess, that could vanquish king Bhagadatta? So also, O
sinless one, all the lords of earth, united together, are incapable, O
Partha, of even gazing at this vast force that is protected by thee. So
also, O Partha, it is owing to their having been always protected by thee
that Dhrishtadyumna and Shikhandi succeeded in slaying Drona and Bhishma.
Who, indeed, O Partha, could vanquish in battle those two mighty
car-warriors of the Bharatas, Bhishma and Drona, both of whom were endued
with prowess equal to that of Sakra himself? Save thee, O tiger among
men, what other man in this world is able to vanquish those fierce lords
of Akshauhinis, those unreturning and invincible heroes, all accomplished
in weapons and united together, Shantanu's son Bhishma, and Drona, and
Vaikartana, and Kripa, and Drona's son, and king Duryodhana himself?
Innumerable divisions of soldiers have been destroyed (by thee), their
steeds and cars and elephants having been mangled (with thy shafts).
Numberless Kshatriyas also, wrathful and fierce, hailing from diverse
provinces, have been destroyed by thee. Teeming with horses and
elephants, large bodies of combatants of diverse Kshatriya clans, such as
the Govasas, the Dasamiyas, the Vasatis, O Bharata, and the Easterners,
the Vatadhanas, and the Bhojas that are very sensitive of their honour,
approaching thee and Bhima, O Bharata, have met with destruction. Of
terrible deeds and exceedingly fierce, the Tusharas, the Yavanas, the
Khasas, the Darvabhisaras, the Daradas, the Sakas, the Kamathas, the
Ramathas, the Tanganas, the Andhrakas, the Pulindas, the Kiratas of fierce
prowess, the Mlecchas, the Mountaineers, and the races hailing from the
sea-side, all endued with great wrath and great might, delighting in
battle and armed with maces, these all--united with the Kurus and
fighting wrathfully for Duryodhana's sake were incapable of being
vanquished in battle by anybody else save thee, O scorcher of foes! What
man, unprotected by thee, could advance, beholding the mighty and
swelling host of the Dhartarashtras arrayed in order of battle? Protected
by thee, O puissant one, the Pandavas, filled with wrath, and penetrating
into its midst, have destroyed that host shrouded with dust and
resembling a swollen sea. Seven days have elapsed since the mighty
Jayatsena, the ruler of the Magadhas, was slain in battle by Abhimanyu.
After that, 10,000 elephants, of fierce feats, that used to follow that
king, were slain by Bhimasena with his mace. After that, other elephants,
and car-warriors, by hundreds, have been destroyed by Bhima in that
exercise of his might. Even thus, O Partha, during the progress of this
awful battle, the Kauravas, with their steeds and car-warriors and
elephants, encountering Bhimasena and thee, O son of Pandu, have from
hence repaired to the region of Death. The van of the Kaurava army, O
Partha, having been struck down by the Pandavas, Bhishma shot showers of
fierce shafts, O sire! Conversant with the highest weapons, he shrouded
the Cedis, the Pancalas, the Karushas, the Matsyas, and the Kaikayas with
the shafts, and deprived them of life! The welkin became filled with
gold-winged and straight coursing shafts, capable of piercing the bodies
of all foes, that issued out of his bow. He slew thousands of
car-warriors, shooting showers of shafts at a time. In all, he slew a
100,000 men and elephants of great might. Abandoning the diverse motions,
each of a new kind, in which they careered, those wicked kings and
elephants, while perishing, destroyed many steeds and cars and elephants.
Indeed, numberless were the shafts that Bhishma shot in battle.
Slaughtering the Pandava host for ten days together, Bhishma made the
terraces of numberless cars empty and deprived innumerable elephants and
steeds of life. Having assumed the form of Rudra or of Upendra in battle,
he afflicted the Pandava divisions and caused a great carnage amongst
them. Desirous of rescuing the wicked Suyodhana who was sinking in a

with all their resources, made a mighty effort, and rushed against that

regarded as the one foremost hero in the world. Encountering him,
Shikhandi, protected by thee, slew that tiger among men with his straight
shafts. Having obtained thee that art a tiger among men (as his foe),
that grandsire is now stretched on a bed of arrows, like Vritra when he
obtained Vasava for his foe. The fierce Drona also slaughtered the
hostile army for five days together. Having made an impenetrable array
and caused many mighty car-warriors to be slain, that great car-warrior
had protected Jayadratha (for some time). Fierce as the Destroyer
himself, he caused a great carnage in the nocturnal battle. Endued with
great valour, the heroic son of Bharadwaja consumed innumerable
combatants with his arrows. At last, encountering Dhrishtadyumna, he
attained to the highest end. If, on that day, thou hadst not checked in
battle all the (Dhartarashtra) car-warriors headed by the Suta's son,
Drona then would never have been slain. Thou heldst in check the whole
Dhartarashtra force. It was for this, O Dhananjaya, that Drona could be
slain by the son of Prishata. What other Kshatriya, save thee, could in
battle achieve such feats for compassing the slaughter of Jayadratha.
Checking the vast (Kaurava) army and slaying many brave kings, thou
killedest king Jayadratha, aided by the might and energy of thy weapons.
All the kings regarded the slaughter of the ruler of the Sindhus to have
been exceedingly wonderful. I, however, do not regard it so; thou didst
it and thou art a great car-warrior. If this vast assemblage of
Kshatriyas, obtaining thee as a foe, suffer extermination in course of
even a whole day, I should, I think, still regard these Kshatriyas to be
truly mighty. When Bhishma and Drona have been slain, the terrible
Dhartarashtra host, O Partha, may be regarded to have lost all its
heroes. Indeed, with all its foremost warriors slain, with its steeds,
cars, and elephants destroyed, the Bharata army looketh today like the
firmament, reft of the Sun, the Moon, and stars. Yonder host of fierce
prowess, O Partha, hath been shorn of its splendours today like the Asura
host in days of yore shorn of its splendours by Sakra's prowess. The
remnant of that grand master now consists of only five great
car-warriors, viz., Ashvatthama, Kritavarma, Karna, Shalya, and Kripa.
Slaying those five great car-warriors today, O tiger among men, be thou a
hero that hath killed all his foes, and bestow thou the Earth with all
her islands and cities on king Yudhishthira. Let Pritha's son
Yudhishthira of immeasurable energy and prosperity, obtain today the
whole earth with the welkin above it, the waters on it, and the nether
regions below it. Slaying this host like Vishnu in days of yore slaying
the Daityas and the Danavas, bestow the Earth on the king like Hari
bestowing (the three worlds) on Sakra. Let the Pancalas rejoice today,
their foes being slain, like the celestials rejoicing after the slaughter
of the Danavas by Vishnu. If in consequence of thy regard for that
foremost of men, viz., thy preceptor Drona, thou cherishest compassion
for Ashvatthama, if, again, thou hast any kindness for Kripa for the sake
of respect that is due to a preceptor, if, approaching Kritavarma, thou
dost not despatch him today to Yama's abode in consequence of the honour
that is due to one's kinsmen by the mother's side, if, O lotus-eyed one,
approaching thy mother's brother, viz., Shalya, the ruler of the Madras,
thou dost not from compassion slay him, I ask thee, do thou, with keen
shafts, O foremost of men slay Karna today with speed, that vile wretch
of sinful heart who cherisheth the fiercest hate for the son of Pandu.
This is thy noblest duty. There is nothing in it that would be improper.
We approve of it, and here is no fault in the act. The wicked-souled
Karna is the root, O thou of unfading glory, of that attempt, O sinless
one, made in the night for burning thy mother with all her children, and
of that conduct which Suyodhana adopted towards you in consequence of
that match at dice. Suyodhana always hopeth for deliverance through
Karna. Filled with rage, he endeavours to afflict me also (in consequence
of that support). It is the firm belief of Dhritarashtra's royal son, O
giver of honours, that Karna, without doubt, will slay all the Prithas in
battle. Though fully acquainted with thy might, still, O son of Kunti,
Dhritarashtra's son hath selected war with you in consequence of his
reliance on Karna. Karna also always says, 'I will vanquish the assembled
Parthas and that mighty car-warrior, viz., Vasudeva of Dasharha's race'.
Buoying up the wicked-souled son of Dhritarashtra, the wicked Karna
always roareth in the (Kuru) assembly. Slay him today, O Bharata. In all

you, the wicked-souled Karna of sinful understanding hath been the
leader. I saw the heroic son of Subhadra of eyes like those of a bull,
slain by six mighty car-warriors of cruel heart belonging to the
Dhritarashtra army. Grinding those bulls among men, viz., Drona, Drona's
son, Kripa and other heroes, he deprived elephants of their riders and
mighty car-warriors of their cars. The bull-necked Abhimanyu, that
spreader of the fame of both the Kurus and the Vrishnis, deprived steeds
also of their riders and foot-soldiers of weapons and life. Routing the
(Kaurava) divisions and afflicting many mighty car-warriors, he
despatched innumerable men and steeds and elephants to Yama's abode. I
swear by Truth to thee, O friend, that my limbs are burning at the
thought that while the son of Subhadra was thus advancing, consuming the
hostile army with his shafts, even on that occasion the wicked-souled
Karna was engaged in acts of hostility to that hero, O lord! Unable, O
Partha, to stay in that battle before Abhimanyu's face, mangled with the
shafts of Subhadra's son, deprived of consciousness, and bathed in blood,"
}

Gandiva and stretching it, he held his bow for the destruction of Karna,
and addressed Keshava, saying, "With thee for my protector, O Govinda,
and when thou that art acquainted with the past and the future art
gratified with me today, victory is sure to be mine. Aided by thee, O
Krishna, I can, in great battle, destroy the three worlds assembled
together, what need be said of Karna then? I see the Pancala host is
flying away, O Janardana. I see also Karna careering fearlessly in
battle. I see too the bhargava weapon careering in all directions, having
been invoked by Karna, O thou of Vrishni's race, like the puissant
thunder invoked by Shakra. This is that battle in which Karna will be
slain by me and of which all creatures will speak as long as the earth
will last. Today, O Krishna, unbarbed arrows, impelled by my arms and
sped from the Gandiva, mangling Karna, will take him to Yama. Today king
Dhritarashtra will curse that intelligence of his in consequence of which
he had installed Duryodhana, who was undeserving of sovereignty, on the
throne. Today, O mighty-armed one, Dhritarashtra will be divested of
sovereignty, happiness, prosperity, kingdom, city, and sons. I tell thee
truly, O Krishna, that today, Karna being slain, Duryodhana will become
hopeless of both life and kingdom. Today, beholding Karna cut in pieces
by me with my arrows, like Vritra in days of yore by Indra in the battle
between the gods and the Asuras, let king Duryodhana call to mind the
words thou hast spoken for bringing about peace. Today let the son of
Subala, O Krishna, know that my shafts are dice, my Gandiva the box for
throwing them, and my car, the chequered cloth. O Govinda, slaying Karna
with keen shafts I will dispel the long sleeplessness of Kunti's son.
Today the royal son of Kunti, upon the slaughter of the Suta's son by me,
shall be gratified and be of cheerful heart and obtain happiness for
ever. Today, O Keshava, I will shoot an irresistible and unrivalled arrow
that will deprive Karna of life. Even this, O Krishna, was the vow of
that wicked-souled one about my slaughter, viz., 'I will not wash my feet
till I slay Phalguna.' Falsifying this vow of that wretch, O slayer of
Madhu, I will, with straight shafts, throw down his body today from his
car. Today the earth will drink the blood of that Suta's son who in
battle condemns all other men on earth! With Dhritarashtra's approbation,
the Suta's son Karna, boasting of his own merits, had said, 'Thou hast no
husband now, O Krishna!' My keen shafts will falsify that speech of his.
Like angry snakes of virulent poison, they will drink his life-blood.
Cloth-yard shafts, of the effulgence of the lightning, shot by myself
possessed of mighty arms, sped from Gandiva, will send Karna on his last
journey. Today the son of Radha will repent for those cruel words that he
said unto the princess of Pancala in the midst of the assembly, in
disparagement of the Pandavas! They that were on that occasion sesame
seeds without kernel, will today become seeds with kernel after the fall
of the Suta's son Karna of wicked soul, otherwise called Vaikartana! 'I
will save ye from the sons of Pandu!'--even these were the words that
Karna, bragging of his own merits, said unto the sons of Dhritarashtra!
My keen shafts will falsify that speech of his! Today, in the very sight
of all the bowmen, I will slay that Karna who said, 'I will slay all the
Pancalas with their sons.' Today, O slayer of Madhu, I will slay that
Karna, that son of Radha, relying on whose prowess the proud son of
Dhritarashtra, of wicked understanding, always disregarded us. Today, O
Krishna, after Karna's fall, the Dhartarashtras with their king, struck
with panic, will fly away in all directions, like deer afraid of the
lion. Today let king Duryodhana repent upon the slaughter of Karna, with
his sons and relatives, by me in battle. Today, beholding Karna slain,
let the wrathful son of Dhritarashtra, O Krishna, know me to be the
foremost of all bowmen in battle. Today, I will make king Dhritarashtra,
with his sons and grandsons and counsellors and servants, shelterless.
Today, cranes and other carnivorous birds will, O Keshava, sport over the
limbs of Karna cut off into pieces with my shafts. Today, O slayer of
Madhu, I will cut off in battle the head of Radha's son Karna, in the
very sight of all the bowmen. Today, O slayer of Madhu, I will cut off in
battle the limbs of Radha's son of wicked soul with keen vipathas and
razor-faced arrows. Today, the heroic king Yudhishthira will cast off a
great pain and a great sorrow cherished long in his heart. Today, O
Keshava, slaying the son of Radha, with all his kinsmen, I will gladden
king Yudhishthira, the son of Dharma. Today, I will slay the cheerless
followers of Karna in battle, with shafts resembling the blazing fire or
the poison of the snake. Today, with my straight shafts equipped with
vulturine feathers, I will, O Govinda, cause the earth to be strewn with
(the bodies of) kings cased in golden armour. Today, O slayer of Madhu, I
will, with keen shafts, crush the bodies and cut off the heads of all the
foes of Abhimanyu. Today, I will bestow the earth, divested of
Dhartarashtras on my brother, or, perhaps, thou, O Keshava, wilt walk
over the earth divested of Arjuna! Today, O Krishna, I will free myself
from the debt I owe to all bowmen, to my own wrath, to the Kurus, to my
shafts, and to Gandiva. Today, I will be freed from the grief that I have

the mighty car-warriors of the Somakas, who are desirous of accomplishing
the task of their allies, regard their task as accomplished. I do not
know what will be the measure, O Madhava, of the joy of Sini's grandson"
